educate.name: Educate
educate.summary: Engaging-explainer arc inspired by Mary Roach: surprise the audience with a fact, walk them through evidence and anecdote, scrutinize the assumptions, then close on a memorable insight. For technical, scientific, or analytical talks that need to feel more like discovery than instruction.

beats.name: Introduction
beats.description: Introduce the topic in a way that respects the audience's time and curiosity. Frame why this question is worth asking, and signal the shape of the journey ahead without giving away the destination.

beats.name: Surprising Fact
beats.description: Lead with a single curious fact that recasts how the audience thinks about the topic. The fact should be small, specific, and unforgettable — the cognitive door the rest of the talk walks through.

beats.name: Experiment
beats.description: Walk through a method, study, or thought experiment that probes the surprising fact. Show how knowledge here gets made — the audience should feel like they're shoulder-to-shoulder with the investigator.

beats.name: Amusing Anecdote
beats.description: Drop in a story or moment from the field that brings the topic to human scale. Personality and humor here keep the audience leaning forward; technical depth without warmth loses the room.

beats.name: Intriguing Information
beats.description: Layer in the more complex data or detail. By this point the audience is invested enough to do real work alongside you. Visualize generously — make the numbers tangible.

beats.name: Skeptical Scrutiny
beats.description: Question the easy interpretations. Challenge the audience's defaults and your own. Showing where the evidence is contested is what separates a teacher from a publicist.

beats.name: Extraordinary Explanation
beats.description: Present the most counterintuitive or beautiful explanation the topic offers. Take your time here — this is the payoff slide the audience came for.

beats.name: Unconventional Use
beats.description: Show an unexpected application or implication of the idea. Surprise reinforces the lesson and gives the audience a story to retell tomorrow.

beats.name: Captivating Conclusion
beats.description: Close with a thoughtful, slightly poetic wrap-up. Echo the surprising fact, name the lesson, and leave the audience with a new question instead of a tidy answer.

media.name: Media & Press
media.summary: Journalists, analysts, and media professionals seeking newsworthy insights and quotable statistics.
media.description: Journalists, analysts, and media professionals looking for newsworthy insight and quotable statistics. Make headline numbers prominent, attribute every figure clearly, design for print, and add embargo notes when needed. Moderate chart density; 8-12 slides in press-kit format.

educate.name: Educate
educate.summary: Teach a concept, process, product, or domain so the audience can use it correctly.
educate.description: Use when the primary job is learning. Structure around concepts, examples, practice, and checks for understanding rather than persuasion or reporting.
educate.outcome: The audience understands the material well enough to apply it.

inspirational.name: Inspirational
inspirational.summary: Aspirational, narrative-driven voice for keynotes, founders, and rallying cries.
inspirational.description: Reach for shared belief and possibility, then ground it in something concrete. Use vivid imagery and rhythm; avoid collapsing into hype by always pairing aspiration with a real anchor.
voiceCues: Open with belief; close with action.
Use rhythm — paired phrases, repetition, deliberate beats.
Pair every aspirational claim with a concrete proof point.
Speak in present tense to make the future feel inevitable.
avoid: Stacked superlatives ('the very best, world-changing, revolutionary').
Dense data tables — push numbers into supporting slides.
samplePhrases: We're building the runtime that makes agents feel instant.
When latency disappears, what becomes possible?
The next decade of software belongs to teams who treat speed as a feature.

minimal.name: Minimal
minimal.description: A clean, minimalistic theme with a focus on simplicity and readability. Ideal for professional, straightforward presentations.

slate-gray.name: Slate Gray
slate-gray.summary: Neutral gray palette for understated executive communication.
slate-gray.description: A disciplined gray scale with strong neutral contrast. Use it when the content should feel calm, mature, and analytical.

cool-horizon.name: Cool Horizon
cool-horizon.summary: Cool blue-green palette tuned for professional business decks.
cool-horizon.description: A balanced cool-toned scheme with deep navy, business blues, and teal accents. It works well across strategy, finance, and technical narratives.

courier-new.name: Courier New
courier-new.description: Courier New is a monospace OPF font scheme for Latin presentations, using Courier New for both headings and body text.

aptos.name: Aptos
aptos.description: Aptos is a sans serif OPF font scheme for Latin presentations, using Aptos Display for headings with Aptos for body text.

title.name: Title
title.summary: Reach for it when the slide is a single headline: a cover, a divider or a one-line statement.
title.description: A title and nothing else. The slide carries one headline with no subtitle or body, so the message is the whole slide.

text-3x.name: Text 3x
text-3x.summary: Reach for it when three parallel points each need a short passage of their own.
text-3x.description: A title above three text blocks in a row, equal in weight. Use it for three pillars, three steps explained in prose, or three options described one by one.

chart-3x.name: Chart 3x
chart-3x.summary: Reach for it when three charts tell one story, each with its own note.
chart-3x.description: A title above three charts, each followed by a text block, in three columns. Use it for a small-multiples view of three metrics, regions or cohorts.

list-6x.name: List 6x
list-6x.summary: Reach for it when six groups of points need parallel lists on one slide.
list-6x.description: A title above six lists in a three-column grid. Use it for six categories or a full inventory in which every group has a few short bullets.
